units: the object described is a listening accessory set down on a piece of furniture
a coloured signal moves across the surface before the charge ends
a short sound announces that the cell is full
the shell carries marks of use along its edges
the hinged joint bends without breaking
the lead stows away in a side compartment
an opening lets the heat out towards the back
the stand can be tilted a step at a time
the whole thing folds down enough to lie at the bottom of a bag
text: Set the earpiece down on the sideboard and watch what follows. The shell warms a little, then a thin blue band creeps across the top, and at last a short chime says the rechargeable cell has taken all it can hold. Pick the case up: it sits in the palm, scuffed along the edges, its soft hinge folding over and over without ever splitting. The lead coils into a pocket in the side, out of the way. Later, once the shell has grown warm, a slotted vent pushes the hot air out at the back. The adjustable stand lifts a notch, then another, until the angle suits you at last. When the session ends, everything closes up again: the folding base slips into its sleeve, the cord follows, and the whole thing goes flat enough to lie at the bottom of a bag. Nothing bulky, nothing brittle, nothing to unscrew.

units: the text asks why electronic equipment wears out so early
a glued assembly stops any single part being replaced on its own
repair workshops see this happening
whole objects are thrown away when one joint alone has failed
makers cut short the period of software support
sound equipment becomes unusable for want of a patch
the buyer carries a double cost
local repairers lose their trade
the writer calls for an assembly that comes apart and drawings anyone can obtain
the writer asks that the cell can be changed on its own
text: Why do our machines wear out so early? Begin with the glue. Once a casing is bonded instead of screwed, no single failed part can be lifted out and replaced on its own. Anyone standing at a repair bench sees it week after week: whole objects carried off to the tip when one joint alone had let go. A second cause makes the first worse. Makers cut short the years of software support, so a sound piece of kit turns useless for want of a patch. The cost falls twice on the buyer, who pays for two machines where one would have served, and the workshop round the corner loses the trade that kept it alive. None of this is settled. Screws rather than adhesive, drawings anyone can obtain, and a rechargeable cell that comes out on its own would hand the repairer back what the glue took away.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure is named by her trade as a repairer
the smell of molten metal stays on her hands after closing time
she started out with old dusty sound receivers
those sets came from a woman living nearby
at first she could not tell which part had failed
she swapped parts at random and spent her money on them
she took up the habit of writing every fault down
her notebook records the symptom and the part to blame
she now recognises recurring families of faults
she repairs almost without ever taking money
text: Her hands hold the smell of molten metal long after the shutters come down. The repairer began on dusty old wireless sets, passed on by a woman who lived along the road, which she opened without a drawing and closed without much faith. Her trouble sat in one sentence: she could not tell which part had given up, so she swapped one for another on a guess and watched her savings go with them. The way out came from a notebook. In it she writes every fault down, the sign it gave, the part to blame, the reading she took. The book has grown thick, stained, soft at the corners from handling. She reads whole families of faults in it now, and guesses before the shell is even open. Neighbours bring her dead lamps and wired keyboards. She gives them back alive, one by one, and mostly refuses to be paid.

units: two soldering devices are compared
one reaches the wanted heat far sooner than the other
that gap weighs on the pace of the workshop
the slower device offers a fine setting of the heat
the quick device gives only a few fixed positions
the heavy base of one holds better
the other shifts as soon as its lead is pulled
the softened lead on one of them soaks up knocks
the other lead stiffens in the cold
one of the two demands costly branded tips
text: Two soldering stations share one bench, and the verdict rests on gaps you can measure. The first brings its tip up to the set temperature almost at once; the second dawdles, and that delay drags on everything the workshop gets through in a day. The slow one, mind you, lets the heat be dialled to the degree, where the quick one offers three fixed positions and nothing in between. One sits on a heavy base, awkward but steady; the other slides the moment its lead is tugged. That lead tells too: supple sheathing on the first soaks up every knock, while the second stiffens in a cold room and passes each jolt straight to the point. One takes ordinary spare tips, the other insists on a costly make of its own. For a repair bench the slow and heavy machine wins in the end, waiting and all.

units: the writer is addressing the manager of a workshop
the message concerns equipment lent to a group
the embroidery machine now takes the designs the club sends over
its arm sags against thick cloth
the jointed support of the lamp no longer holds its height
the tablet works only once it is plugged into the mains
its cell no longer lasts a whole session
the trolley unit blocks the way through the room
two typing peripherals are missing from the store cupboard
the writer asks that these remarks be passed on to the technical service
text: Dear workshop manager, I am writing about the equipment lent to the assisted sewing group. First, the embroidery machine now takes the designs the club sends over, though its arm sags as soon as the cloth is at all thick. Second, the jointed lamp gives good light, but its adjustable neck will no longer stay in the high position. Third, the tablet lent to the learners remains usable provided it is left plugged in: its rechargeable cell no longer lasts half a session. Fourth, the trolley unit is too bulky for the room and blocks the way through. Lastly, two wired keyboards have gone from the dusty cupboard at the back. I should be grateful if you would pass these remarks on to the technical service, and I remain available for any checking you may wish to have carried out.

units: a visitor asks a workshop how an electronic board is made
the layout is drawn on screen first
the pattern is carried onto a metal-coated board by exposure to light
the unwanted metal is taken off in a chemical bath
a guided rotary tool drills the ways meant for the connections
a solder paste is laid down before the parts are set in place
the whole thing is taken up to a high heat to fix the joints
a camera looks over every board for a flaw
this check comes before the final assembly
text: A visitor to the workshop asks first how a printed board comes into being. The answer follows the order of the work. At the outset a layout is drawn on screen, then carried onto a metal-coated plate by exposure to light. The visitor asks next what becomes of the metal nobody wants. It is eaten away in a chemical bath, and the plate comes out with its tracks clean and fine. Then comes the drilling: a guided cutter opens the ways where the pins will sit. Is the plate ready to use, the visitor wonders. Not yet, because solder paste must be laid down, the parts set down in place, and the whole thing taken up to a heat that fixes every joint. A last question turns on the way the work is checked. Each board passes under a camera that catches the faulty track before the final assembly.

units: a man from the floor above complains about how long his drilling tool lasts
his neighbour puts the fault down to the way the tool is charged
the power pack was left sitting on its charger all the time
the casing of the pack had swollen out of shape
a measuring device was used to test the cells one by one
two cells no longer gave any current
that explains the loss of force while drilling
he is advised to store the pack half charged and somewhere cool
he must take it off the charger as soon as the green light shows
text: The man from the flat upstairs came down with his drill under his arm, saying the battery would hold nothing at all any more. My sister told him the tool was not to blame, and that it came of his habit of leaving the rechargeable pack sitting on its hot base day and night. He argued for a while, then owned up that the casing had swollen out of shape. So she fetched a wired meter out of the dusty drawer and tested each cell on its own, one after the other. Two of them gave nothing back at all, which explained why the drill lost its bite the moment the bit met the wood. Keep the pack half charged, she told him, somewhere cool, and take it off the charger as soon as the green light shows. He went back upstairs pleased, with a drill that ran again and a fresh bit into the bargain.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first mechanical looms ran into the same blockage over and over
changing the pattern meant taking the mechanism apart
the threads had to be set back one by one
work stopped for several weeks
customers turned to the weavers who worked by hand
the answer was to hold the pattern outside the machine
a craftsman thought of a run of pierced boards laced together
whether a hole was there or not decided if the thread rose
altering the design came down to changing the band
calculating devices took the same principle up later
text: In the earliest mechanised weaving sheds one obstacle came round again and again. Changing the design meant taking the mechanism apart and setting every thread back in its place one at a time, and the work stood still for whole weeks together. Orders drifted off to the weavers who still worked by hand, slower but far more biddable. The answer came from outside the trade altogether: hold the pattern in something that sits apart from the machine. A craftsman thought of small pierced boards, laced into a supple band that the loom read as it went by. Where a needle met a hole, the thread rose; elsewhere it stayed where it lay. Altering the design now came down to changing the band. The idea soon outgrew cloth, and the calculating machines that followed still work on that same split.

units: the aerial is likened to a string that trembles as a wave goes past
the aerial makes no energy of its own
the loudspeaker runs the other way round
a current sets the cone of the loudspeaker moving
that movement shakes the air around it
in one case the energy arrives from outside and turns electrical
in the other it leaves the wire and turns into sound
neither device bears a harsh setting well
a magnetised mass of metal bends the signal
text: An aerial is less like an ear than like a taut string stretched over an invisible river. The string makes nothing of its own: it trembles while a wave goes past, and it falls quiet once the wave has moved off. A loudspeaker runs the other way round. Send a current into it, its soft cone stirs, and the air about it begins to shake. One listens, the other speaks, and both live off the same family of movements. The difference lies in which way the exchange runs. In the aerial the energy arrives from outside and turns into a faint current; in the loudspeaker it leaves the wire and turns into something you can hear. One more thing draws them together: neither bears a harsh setting. A rigid mount kills the movement, a magnetised mass bends the signal, and ear and mouth alike go deaf.

units: a failure comes up at night on a backup server
the team goes through three areas in turn
the power supply shows an odd swing in voltage
a worn capacitor lies behind that fault
a fan no longer turns evenly
its clogged bearing lets the temperature pass the allowed limit
two storage units carry areas that cannot be read
no warning had been raised about those areas
the parts at fault are replaced and the data rebuilt
the lesson drawn is that a silent fault costs more
text: The fault broke out in the middle of a maintenance night, on a backup server the team had taken for indestructible. Three lines of enquiry were worked through in order. On the power side, the reading showed an odd ripple on the main rail, the mark of a worn and swollen capacitor. On cooling, a failing fan turned in fits and starts, and its clogged bearing let the board run well beyond the temperature allowed. On storage, two drives carried sectors that could no longer be read, and no warning about them had ever come through. The repair followed the same list: capacitor renewed, fan swapped for one with a smoother bearing, drives rebuilt onto the array. The team came away from that night with a lesson that has stuck. A fault that says nothing costs far more than one that makes a noise.
